topic: The Elastic Collision Pi-Calculator: From Physics to Mathematics
target_audience: University students (Physics/Math majors or CS enthusiasts)

sections.title: Introduction: The Paradox of Particles
sections.content: Introduce the physical setup: two blocks on a frictionless surface. Block A has mass M, Block B has mass 100^N * M. Both undergo perfectly elastic collisions. Pose the question: How many collisions occur before the blocks stop moving toward each other?
sections.example: A small rabbit (Mass 1kg) facing a giant elephant (Mass 10,000kg). If the rabbit hits the elephant, how many 'bounces' occur until the elephant is moving away?

sections.title: Prerequisite Physics: Conservation Laws
sections.content: Briefly review Conservation of Momentum and Conservation of Kinetic Energy. Explain that for elastic collisions, the state (velocity) transformation can be represented as a 2D rotation matrix.
sections.example: Visualize the state space as a coordinate system where velocity vectors (v1, v2) rotate by a fixed angle determined by the mass ratio, effectively 'bouncing' off a slanted line in the phase plane.

sections.title: Connecting Collisions to Pi
sections.content: Explain the mapping: The total number of collisions corresponds to the digits of PI. As the mass ratio increases (100, 10,000, 1,000,000...), the geometry of the collision space mimics the circumference of a circle.
sections.example: Show an animation where the collision path traces a discrete 'zig-zag' pattern inside an angular wedge. As the mass ratio approaches infinity, the path smooths into a circle arc covering PI radians.

sections.title: Visualization and Scaling
sections.content: Demonstrate the digit generation: For a mass ratio of 100^N, the number of collisions reveals the first N+1 digits of Pi (e.g., 100^0 -> 3; 100^1 -> 31; 100^2 -> 314).
sections.example: A graphic animation showing a 'collision counter' ticking up. A mass ratio of 100^2 results in 314 total collisions—the famous approximation of Pi.

sections.title: Conclusion: The Beauty of Abstraction
sections.content: Summarize how physical conservation laws act as a 'computer' to calculate transcendental numbers. Emphasize that what looks like a simple mechanical problem is actually an encoding of circular geometry.
sections.example: Closing visual: A galaxy of blocks colliding, with the digits '3.14159...' emerging as the final count of the cosmic dance.
